title: Using generative AI for dialogue in narrative games without losing character consistency
author: AimaiStudio
selftext:
I’m working on an indie, browser-based narrative game where generative AI is used **o**nly for dialogue, not for asset or story generation.

The main challenge I’ve been focused on is *long-term character consistency* in a game context, especially when conversations are spread across many sessions and tied to progression.

Some constraints I’m currently using:

* Hand-authored character profiles (personality, tone, boundaries)
* Fixed backstory milestones unlocked by progression
* External memory structures for key facts and emotional beats
* AI restricted to moment-to-moment dialogue only (no world-building or major plot decisions)

What I’ve found interesting is that:

* Players tolerate imperfection
* But they immediately notice *emotional or personality drift*
* A single out-of-character response can break immersion faster than obvious “AI-ness”

I’m curious how others here are handling similar problems in game development contexts:

* Do you rely more on system prompts or structured memory?
* How do you handle emotional continuity over time?
* Have you found effective ways to prevent gradual personality collapse in long-running interactions?

I’m sharing this from my own project (Aimai) as context, but mainly hoping to compare approaches and learn from others experimenting with generative AI in narrative or interactive systems.

Happy to go deeper into implementation details if useful.

comments.author: MatsutakeShinji
comments.body: Do you generate dialogs with AI on-the-fly or pre-generate them and use as static assets?

replies.author: AimaiStudio
replies.body:
Dialogue is generated on-the-fly, but within strict constraints.

Character archetypes, personality traits, boundaries, and key backstory milestones are hand-authored and stored in structured data (JSON). The model doesn’t invent major facts or progression, it only fills in moment-to-moment dialogue based on those constraints and the current context.

Anything persistent (important memories, emotional beats, unlocked story points) is stored outside the model and fed back in, so continuity comes from structure rather than raw generation.

replies.author: CultureContent8525
replies.body: Won't it be overkill if players starts playing the game seriously at scale? Won't the token consumption be off the charts?

replies.author: AimaiStudio
replies.body:
That’s a fair concern, and it’s something I’ve thought about a lot. The key is that AI isn’t used for everything.

Most structure is fixed and hand-authored (character profiles, progression gates, memories, story beats). The model only generates moment-to-moment dialogue.

At scale, the plan is to combine tighter context windows, summarization of older conversations, and selective generation so the system isn’t just brute-forcing tokens nonstop. The goal is sustainable interaction, not unlimited freeform chat.

comments.author: -goldenboi69-
comments.body: Sounds like it will get expensive fast?

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: It does. Every AI dev wants to implement this, but it's not feasible for indies.

comments.author: buzzspinner
comments.body: If you’re talking about token usage, you can use open source ai models through a gui like ComfyAI for free if your computer is decent

replies.author: tomqmasters
replies.body: Local models that run on mid tear gaming computers are not very good.

replies.author: buzzspinner
replies.body: Or take forever. Im still in the experimental phase

comments.author: cleanscholes
comments.body: Make sure you're compressing before the context gets too long. Go look up degradation curves with respect to the size of the context window and you'll see what I mean.

comments.author: No-Possession-7095
comments.body: For emotional continuity i assign a sentiment score for each NPC in relation to the player.  This then dictates all sorts of things on regard to how they will respond.  I use both prompts and database for memory.   I implemented this in the adventure selection in this game reachtothestars.com.

comments.author: SassFrog
comments.body:
You could use LLMs to generate a first pass of dialogue from context which is curated and refined over time. That seems realistic given the current state of the technology for a narrative game that isn't dogshit. Tracery and Gamygdala come to mind as useful frameworks to generating a massive set of prompts/context for generating a first pass of dialogue.

https://github.com/broekens/gamygdala
https://github.com/galaxykate/tracery
